_note: The [[SCALE]] size-ladder test for describer_object. Built session 24, BEFORE the ladder reaches the prompt -- describer_object v3 still has free-text [[SCALE]] and the fixed 'worn on the body' for garments, so running this against v3 measures the field being replaced and every case will 'miss'. That is expected and is not a signal. The key exists first on purpose: .claude/TODO.md requires the key and the vocabulary be built together rather than the key being retro-fitted to whatever the prompt turned out to say. Score with: python scripts/score.py tests/describer_object_scale.json runs/run-*.txt --fields SCALE
_the_ladder: Nine terms, ONE axis: bulk compared to an ADULT body. The bottom four rungs use the hand and forearm as RULERS, never as a grip -- how many hands hold a thing is an affordance of its handle, not a fact about its size, and describer_object.txt separately forbids recording how a thing is held at all. minuscule (fits inside a closed adult fist: a coin, a key, a ring) < tiny (no bigger than an open adult hand: a phone, a banknote) < small (bigger than a hand, up to about a forearm: a cereal box, a frying pan, a shoulder bag, a portable radio) < modest (bigger than a forearm, but plainly less bulk than an adult body: a suitcase, a tower computer, a microwave, an end table, a small dining chair, a child's ride-on car) < medium (comparable to an adult body -- about three-quarters of adult height or more, or big enough to enclose or seat one adult: an adult human, an executive office chair, a wheelie bin, a bumper car) < large (clearly more than one adult, up to A CAR: any car, a sofa, a horse) < huge (bigger than a car, smaller than A HOUSE: a van, a lorry, a bus) < gargantuan (a house up to a large building: an apartment block, a ship, an airliner) < colossal (bigger than any ordinary building: a skyscraper, a mountain).
_no_rung_is_defined_by_how_a_thing_is_HE: Found session 24, after the ladder was drafted and before it shipped. An early draft read small as 'needs two adult hands' and modest as 'carried with both arms'. That is an AFFORDANCE, not a size: a frying pan is about two hands across but has a handle and is held with one; a cereal box likewise; a suitcase without a handle needs both arms and with one does not. Worse, it contradicts this role's own headline rule -- describer_object.txt bans recording how a thing is shown, naming 'held, carried' explicitly -- so the model would have been told never to note how a thing is held and then asked to size it by exactly that. The bottom four rungs now use the hand and forearm as RULERS (how much hand does it span) rather than as grips (how many hands hold it). See L-A-RUNG-BOUND-MUST-BE-A-FIXED-SIZE.
_every_comparison_is_to_an_adult: THE RULE MOST LIKELY TO BE QUIETLY VIOLATED when the ladder is written into the prompt. The words 'a person', 'a human' (unqualified), 'someone' and 'a child' must NEVER appear in a rung definition. A child IS a person, so 'smaller than a person' silently admits 'smaller than a toddler' -- which inverts the modest/medium boundary, and the cases that force that boundary (obsc_modest_1, obsc_modest_2) are precisely the ones with a child in frame. This is L-UNDEFINED-TERMS-READ-AS-OBVIOUS.
_boundaries_are_named_from_both_sides: Every interior boundary is closed by the same object from below and opened by it from above: A CAR closes large and opens huge; A HOUSE closes huge and opens gargantuan. That is what removes the gap the earlier draft had, where huge had no ceiling at all and gargantuan was defined by an occupancy count ('holds hundreds') that contradicted its own 'a house' exemplar. Occupancy is a TELL, never a definition.
_occupancy_is_a_tell_bulk_is_the_axis: 'Could an adult be enclosed or seated by it' decides hollow things; solid things go on comparable bulk. This is what separates a small dining chair (seats an adult, nowhere near their bulk -> modest) from an executive office chair (about three-quarters of adult height and encloses one -> medium). A pure occupancy test fails that pair. A pure HEIGHT test fails obsc_bumper_car, which is adult-LENGTH but low.
_gate_why: Stocked to hit every rung by construction, so the failure rate carries no information about the corpus and the level gate would be meaningless. Gate on MOVEMENT: pass --baseline <previous round of THIS test>. Note there is no baseline yet -- the first scored round establishes one, and its own verdict is 'adjudicate, cap 6' per CLAUDE.md's enriched-first-run rule.
_flagship_pair: obsc_minuscule and obsc_smart_car are THE SAME CAR MODEL -- a red-over-black two-seat city car -- once as a die-cast toy pinched between finger and thumb, once full size at a kerb. Five rungs apart on visually near-identical subjects. If one pair is worth reading first, it is this one: it isolates physical size from every other cue, and it is the direct test of the standing rule that [[SCALE]] describes the thing actually photographed, never the thing it depicts.
_distractor_pair: obsc_car_palace and obsc_car_mountain are keyed `large` DELIBERATELY, and this is not a mistake in the filenames. Both images were supplied to exercise gargantuan and colossal, but a palace is a place and a mountain is terrain -- describer_object.txt forbids describing the environment ('Do NOT describe the ENVIRONMENT, background, setting'), and REF2VA's role selector routes both to describer_setting. Asking this role for SUBJECT: the mountain would ask it to break its own rule. So the RED CAR is the subject in each, and what these two now test is that an enormous backdrop does not drag [[SCALE]] up a ladder anchored on absolute adult comparison rather than on share of frame.
_colossal_is_unexercised: No case keys `colossal`, and probably none ever can in this role: everything colossal is terrain or architecture, which describer_setting owns. The user notes the only conceivable filler is a sci-fi spaceship, with no real-world example -- even the ISS reads gargantuan. This is admissible under docs/image_inventory.md 'Adding a term the corpus cannot exercise', whose precondition is that the tell be STATABLE, and here it is: 'bigger than any ordinary building'. Recorded as a deliberate decision, not an oversight.
_watched_seam: modest/medium, via obsc_modest_1 and obsc_modest_2. TODO.md named small/modest/medium as the ladder's weakest seam before any of these images existed: in ordinary English 'modest' and 'medium' both mean middling, and the model has a strong D&D prior for every term EXCEPT modest. Both cases have a CHILD sitting in the vehicle, which is the nearest human reference in frame and invites 'fits a child -> person-sized -> medium'. They are keyed STRICTLY, with no accept-set, deliberately: pre-forgiving a failure not yet observed would violate L-AN-ACCEPT-SET-IS-A-HYPOTHESIS and would leave `modest` with only obsc_kaypro as a strict sample. IF BOTH MISS TO `medium`, that is the vocabulary failing and it is one finding, not two bad cases.
_vehicle_bias: 16 of the 43 cases are the session-24 batch, and they are almost all red vehicles. That uniformity is the point -- it holds subject family and colour constant so that size is the only variable -- but it means a pass on them evidences nothing about a microwave, a suitcase or a banknote. The non-vehicle evidence is the eleven session-24 imports (obsc_phone, obsc_banknote, obsc_cereal_box, obsc_kaypro, obsc_chair, obsc_wheelie_bin, obsc_cannon, obsc_car_1, obsc_car_2, obsc_jumpsuit_real, obsc_april_figure) plus the sixteen session-25 garment cases (obsc_g_*). Read those as the generalisation check. Note the two halves check different things: the imports spread across the OBJECT rungs, while the garment block is the only GARMENT evidence below `medium` -- before session 25 this file's only garments were obsc_jumpsuit_real and obsc_april_figure, both at the top of the garment range. `minuscule` still has exactly one case in the file and no garment at all.
_large_is_oversampled_on_purpose: Seven of 43 cases key `large` -- 26 percent of the file before session 25, 16 percent after the sixteen garment cases diluted it. The oversampling is therefore weaker than it was, and if `large` ever needs to be the dominant rung again that is a reason to split the garment block into its own file rather than to add more cars. The oversampling is deliberate: `large` is the pivot the whole ladder is defined against, since `huge` means 'bigger than a car'. obsc_car_1 and obsc_car_2 are strict controls and are ALSO an existing same-object angle pair (the corpus's `car-angle` probe), so they double as a drift check -- one object, two viewpoints, and [[SCALE]] must not move. obsc_cannon is WATCHED rather than a control: the user places it on the small side of `large`, and it is the rung's only non-vehicle sample.
_world_knowledge_ruling: obsc_banknote and obsc_phone are isolated shots with little in frame to judge size against. Under a closed ladder they are `tiny` because we know what banknotes and phones ARE, not because the pixels show it. That is a deliberate ruling: [[SCALE]] is a TYPE judgement where the frame offers no reference, which is what stops 'not determinable' absorbing every isolated shot (it took 4 of 24 in the v3 round). It does NOT license depiction-over-physical -- see _depiction_vs_physical, which is a separate rule.
_depiction_vs_physical: The open question, and the ONLY place it arises in the corpus. obsc_april_figure is a photograph of moulded figures; obsc_jumpsuit_real is the same garment on a full-size adult. The standing rule (describe the thing actually photographed) and the corpus both favour `tiny`, so `tiny` is primary and `medium` is forgiven. obsc_jumpsuit_real is the strict control that keeps the set honest: it is the SAME SUBJECT LINE on an unambiguously adult-worn garment, so if the accept-set is quietly collapsing the distinction it will show up there.
_garment_rule: A garment is sized by the PART OF THE BODY IT IS CUT TO COVER, on the body it is cut for -- not by the fabric's bulk, and not by whoever happens to wear it in this picture. This is not a carve-out: a covered body region is a fraction of an adult body, which is the ladder's existing axis, so garments and objects ride the same ruler and no tenth value exists. It is a POINTING rule, the same shape as the one [[SCALE]] already carries ('describes the physical thing photographed, never what it depicts'). On an adult body: a hand or a foot -> tiny (a glove, an ankle sock); a foot and calf, a head, or a forearm's worth -> small (a knee sock, a shoe, a hat); the upper torso, the lower torso and/or the legs but NOT the whole body -> modest (a t-shirt, a vest top, a polo, a one-piece swimsuit, shorts, trousers, a skirt, a jacket); essentially the WHOLE body -> medium (a jumpsuit, a full-length coat, a uniform, a suit of armour). THE SEAM IS WHOLE-BODY VS NOT, AND IT IS DELIBERATELY COARSE: a t-shirt covers the upper torso, a swimsuit covers upper AND lower, trousers cover the lower torso AND the legs -- all three are modest. Only torso and legs together reaches medium. Fabric quantity never enters, which is why the swimsuit is modest alongside the t-shirt despite far less cloth.
_garment_body_size: The rung is taken on THE BODY THE GARMENT IS CUT FOR, using the existing closed age vocabulary (docs/image_inventory.md 'The tokens', nine brackets, imported by inventory.py from validate.py's AGE_PERSON). `teenager` / `young adult` / `adult` / `middle-aged` / `older adult` are ONE adult size -- age above the teenage line never changes the rung. That clause is load-bearing rather than theoretical: six of the main object test's fifteen garment rows are Kasia, whom the corpus records as `teenager`. `pre-teen` / `child` / `toddler` / `infant` are judged on that smaller body, against the same rungs. Sub-teen bodies COMPRESS the region distinctions -- a whole-body garment lands `small` and a top lands `small` too. That compression is a real property of the rule, not a defect, and it is why the toddler image's value is the CROSS-image pair with obsc_g_top_flat rather than an internal one. NOTE THAT THIS RULE MUST USE THE WORD 'child', WHICH RUNG DEFINITIONS BAN: the ban recorded in _every_comparison_is_to_an_adult applies to rung BOUNDS, where 'smaller than a person' silently admits 'smaller than a toddler' and inverts modest/medium. Here 'child' names a body bracket explicitly, which is the opposite failure mode. Do not 'fix' it.
_garment_rule_replaced_a_defect: Session 25. The session-24 ladder said 'garments take their WEARER's size (medium for an adult)'. THAT IS NOT A SIZE -- it is a pointer to a different object. A sock's wearer is an adult; the sock is not adult-sized; an adult's t-shirt is roughly half an adult's bulk. The clause silently assumed every garment covers a whole adult, throwing away variation that is real, visible and permanent. THE DAMAGE WAS IN THE OTHER TEST, NOT THIS ONE: the fifteen garment rows it keyed uniformly `medium` are the ground truth for tests/describer_object.json, staged in the session-22 handoff table, and eight of those fifteen moved to `modest` in session 25. It is the FOURTH instance of the L-A-RUNG-BOUND-MUST-BE-A-FIXED-SIZE defect class in this one vocabulary, and the worst-caught of the four: session 24 hunted for exactly this defect and declared the ladder CLEAN, because the check was a grep for 'a person' / 'a human' / 'someone' / 'a child' and the garment clause said WEARER -- the same failure in a word the grep did not know. See L-VERIFY-THE-PROPERTY-NOT-THE-WORDING. The two pre-existing garment cases (obsc_jumpsuit_real, obsc_april_figure) survive the repair UNCHANGED, so only the prose was ever wrong, not the key.
_garment_minimal_pairs: Three pairs carry the rule, and they are what to read first. (1) BODY SIZE, SAME IMAGE -- obsc_g_infant_bodysuit `small` against obsc_g_adult_polo `modest`: ONE photograph, two garments, one rung apart, with medium, lighting and presentation all held constant so the only variable is whose body. Note the inversion it tests: the infant garment covers MORE of its body yet keys LOWER than the adult garment covering less, so a model reading region while ignoring body size gets this exactly backwards. (2) BODY SIZE, CROSS-IMAGE -- obsc_g_toddler_top `small` against obsc_g_top_flat `modest`: the same garment type (a top, upper torso) on a toddler and on a teenager. (3) REGION, SAME IMAGE -- obsc_g_gloves_flat `tiny` through obsc_g_shorts_flat `modest`: five garments off ONE flat-lay spanning three rungs, holding wearer, medium and presentation constant so that only the covered region varies.
_garment_presentation_drift: Two blocks, deliberately in different media families, both keyed identically to their flat or photographic partner so that drift scores as a MISS rather than needing an eye. KASIA: obsc_g_{gloves,top}_{flat,cel,render} -- the same two garments as flat-lay photograph, 2D cel and 3D CG. UNIFORM: obsc_g_usocks_{photo,anime,painterly} -- knee socks as photograph, anime painting and painterly painting. These are what catch a model sizing the FABRIC AS PRESENTED rather than the region, which is the failure the fabric-bulk reading of the garment rule was rejected for, and nothing else in this file tests it. READ THEM AS BLOCKS: one garment moving between presentations is noise; a whole block moving is that reading asserting itself.
_subject_lines_must_not_name_the_wearer: NO `SUBJECT:` LINE IN A GARMENT CASE MAY NAME WHO WEARS THE THING. It is `the white bodysuit`, never `the infant's bodysuit`; `the corduroy dungarees`, never `the toddler's dungarees`. Naming the wearer hands the model the body-size answer, which is the whole thing under test. It is also the same leak as the v2 subject-supplies defect that describer_object.txt's 'THE SUBJECT LINE SELECTS; IT NEVER SUPPLIES' section was written to fix. Select by colour or material only, and check this before adding any further garment case here.
_garment_watched_seams: For the first scored round. (1) THE FLAT-LAY HAS NO BODY IN FRAME -- kasia_outfit is a flat-lay, so the model must infer the body from the garment's own cut alone. That is the honest hard case for the body-size clause, and where it should fail first if it fails at all. (2) obsc_g_shoes_flat SITS ON THE tiny/small BOUND -- a teen sneaker is only a little past an open adult hand. Missing to `tiny` alone is one case; missing together with obsc_g_socks_flat makes the bottom BOUND the finding rather than the two cases. (3) The reading rejected at the bottom was 'a foot is about a hand, so all footwear is tiny', which would have keyed a thigh boot the same as an ankle sock -- the fabric-vs-region tension reappearing at the bottom of the ladder instead of the middle.

obsc_phone.why: strict control for the obsc_april_figure accept-set: unambiguously one-hand sized, with no depiction reading available at all

obsc_jumpsuit_real.why: strict control for the obsc_april_figure accept-set: the SAME garment and the SAME subject line, worn by a full-size adult, where no depiction reading is available

obsc_april_figure.why: depiction vs physical. `tiny` under the standing rule (the moulded figures actually photographed) and per docs/image_inventory.md, which classifies this file stop-motion / figure 'classified by the objects'. `medium` is forgiven for the reading that treats it as an in-scale diorama element depicting an adult. Anything else -- small, modest, large -- is still a miss.
